claims.text: Mechanical wear at elevated temperature removes the protective native oxide from phase boundaries.
Oxide removal exposes dissimilar phases having distinct electrochemical potentials.
The exposed dissimilar phases form localized galvanic couples.
Corrosion weakens the microstructure and increases its susceptibility to further mechanical wear.
The interaction between galvanically accelerated corrosion and wear creates a positive-feedback tribocorrosion cycle.
The as-cast multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy contains distinct electrochemically active phases.
The initial alloy surface has a native passive oxide layer.
A surface barrier coating or electrochemical passivation treatment will minimize interfacial galvanic coupling.
Coated specimens will have lower total degradation than uncoated specimens under otherwise identical wear-corrosion conditions.
Coated specimens will exhibit lower wear-scar volumes than the uncoated baseline.
Coated specimens will exhibit slower corrosion rates than the uncoated baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies at approximately 600 degrees Celsius in a chloride-rich corrosive environment under active wear sufficient to remove the native oxide.
The proposed mechanism requires distinct electrochemically active phases capable of forming galvanic couples after oxide removal.
The magnitude of degradation reduction depends on coating efficiency, phase distribution, and oxide-removal kinetics.
